title: From the NHS to New Scotland Yard: How an Indian-Origin Finance Chief Landed One of Britain's Most Consequential Public-Sector Roles
excerpt: Hardev Virdee, a marathon runner and award-winning NHS finance director, will lead strategy and investment at the Metropolitan Police as it faces a yawning budget gap and a mandate to reform.
body:
When Hardev Virdee starts his new job at New Scotland Yard, the emails waiting for him will not be about patient-bed ratios or NHS waiting lists. They will be about knife-crime statistics, officer attrition, and a metropolitan police force that serves nine million Londoners but cannot balance its books.

Virdee has been appointed Chief Strategy and Investment Officer of the Metropolitan Police Service — the largest police force in the United Kingdom and one of the most scrutinised law-enforcement bodies in the world. The appointment, announced on 19 May by Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley, makes Virdee one of the most senior Indian-origin figures in British policing.

A Track Record Built in the Trenches of the NHS

The appointment is not a diversity hire dressed up in corporate language. Virdee's credentials are formidable. He spent over a decade in NHS finance, most recently as Group Chief Financial Officer at Barts Health NHS Trust — the largest NHS trust in England, overseeing five hospitals across east London. At Barts, he was credited with turning around a chronic deficit, delivering a financial recovery plan that finally balanced the trust's books in the 2025–26 financial year.

That work earned him recognition well beyond hospital corridors. Virdee won the NHS Director of Finance of the Year award for his role as Chair of the NHS National Finance Academy, a body responsible for developing the next generation of public-sector financial leaders across Britain. He currently serves as Vice President of the Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) — the professional body for public-sector accountants — and is set to take up its presidency this summer.

Why the Met Needs Him Now

The Metropolitan Police is in the middle of the most far-reaching reform programme in its history. A 2023 report by Baroness Casey described the force as institutionally racist, misogynistic, and homophobic. Commissioner Rowley, who took charge in 2022, has been tasked with overhauling the institution — but reform costs money, and the Met's finances are under severe strain.

The force faces what Rowley himself has described as a "significant financial gap," exacerbated by rising demand, inflation-driven cost increases, and a recruitment pipeline struggling to replace officers leaving faster than they can be trained. Virdee's mandate is to lead the Met's long-term strategic planning, prioritise resources, and build relationships with government and funding partners to keep reform on track.

"I am looking forward to welcoming Hardev to the Met bringing his expertise, energy, and insight to support officers and staff," Rowley said. "He was hugely impressive in the selection process — and that was not just the opinion of the panel I chaired, but also one of more junior colleagues."

Virdee, for his part, struck a characteristically understated tone. "Having worked in the NHS for many years, I am excited to continue my commitment to public service," he said. "This is a challenging role, and I look forward to working closely with colleagues and partners to deliver the Met's vision."

The Diaspora Dimension

Virdee's appointment comes at a moment when Indian-origin professionals are occupying an expanding footprint in British public life — from Rishi Sunak's time as Prime Minister to senior roles across the judiciary, the Bank of England, and the civil service. But representation in policing has lagged. A 2024 report by the National Police Chiefs' Council found that while Black and Asian officers make up roughly 10% of the rank and file nationally, they remain sharply underrepresented at the most senior levels.

Virdee's role is not an operational policing position — he will not be making decisions about stop-and-search or public-order deployments. But as the person controlling the Met's purse strings and long-term strategy, he will shape the institutional priorities that determine how London is policed for years to come.

For the estimated 1.9 million people of Indian origin in Britain — many of them Londoners whose relationship with the Met has historically been complex — the symbolism matters. So does the substance.

Outside work, Virdee is a marathon runner. Given the size of the task ahead, the stamina will come in handy.
